name: SynapTech ReadRoom Pro Social Cue Implant
body_location: cranial — processing node at the posterior temporal lobe junction; micro-sensor array embedded in both orbital ridges for gaze and micro-expression capture
description:
The ReadRoom Pro is a two-component system: a pair of micro-optical sensors embedded in the orbital ridge bone beneath the eyebrow line, and a neural processing node implanted at the junction of the posterior temporal and parietal lobes — a region densely involved in social cognition and facial recognition. The orbital sensors capture high-resolution data on the faces and bodies of people within conversational range: micro-expressions lasting as little as 1/25th of a second, postural shifts, gaze direction, pupil dilation, and subtle proxemic adjustments. The processing node runs SynapTech's SocialGraph inference engine, which correlates this data stream against a continuously updated behavioral model and delivers interpretive overlays as soft perceptual impressions — not text or visual HUD elements, but felt intuitions that arrive in the user's awareness like a natural social sense, just sharper and faster. The system can flag discomfort, deception indicators, interest, distraction, and dominance-submission dynamics without interrupting the user's conscious processing.

The ReadRoom Pro was originally developed as a therapeutic tool for autistic adults and people with social anxiety disorders, and it remains one of the most widely prescribed implants in that community. Clinics that specialize in neurodivergent support often subsidize or finance it. But its user base has expanded far beyond its therapeutic origins — sales representatives, educators, negotiators, social workers, customer-facing service workers, and ordinary people who simply find social situations exhausting all use it to reduce the cognitive load of reading a room. Users consistently describe the experience not as receiving information but as feeling more present and less lost in social interactions. Critics raise concerns about consent — conversations now involve one party with enhanced social perception that the other party may not know about — and several GLMZ jurisdictions have begun drafting disclosure requirements for professional use.
legality: Licensed — requires brief consultation with a certified installer; professional deployment in some industries requires disclosure
installation_requirements: Specialist clinic required for orbital sensor placement; cranial node installation is a 90-minute outpatient procedure under local anesthetic with 24-hour rest recommendation
maintenance: SocialGraph model updates monthly via wireless sync; annual calibration of orbital sensors; processor node assessed every 2 years

side_effects: First two to three weeks can be emotionally overwhelming — users report hypersensitivity to others' distress before the system's filtering calibrates to their comfort threshold
Occasional mild headaches during the initial 10-day neural integration period
Some users experience difficulty 'turning off' social awareness in private, leading to fatigue in high-density environments without using the system's manual dampening mode
Rare cases of orbital ridge micro-tenderness persisting for up to 8 weeks post-installation
cultural_context: The ReadRoom Pro occupies a complex social position in GLMZ. In neurodivergent communities, it carries almost no stigma at all — it is understood as a sensory aid, no more remarkable than corrective lenses, and wearing one is widely visible through the faint orbital ridge contour the sensors create. In professional environments, it is increasingly common and largely accepted, though the question of disclosure is genuinely contested. Some people find it deeply uncomfortable to interact with a ReadRoom user, feeling surveilled or at a disadvantage; others argue that skilled social readers have always existed and the implant simply democratizes that ability. Among Tier 1 populations, the licensed price point puts it just out of reach for many, and gray-market ReadRoom units with older SocialGraph models are common — they work, but their inference models are less accurate and more prone to false positives, which can cause their own social problems.

Educators and childcare workers managing large groups
People returning to social environments after long periods of isolation or trauma
story_hooks: A player character with a ReadRoom Pro begins receiving anomalous impression-data during conversations with a specific individual — signals that don't match any human behavioral model in SocialGraph, as though the person's micro-expressions are being artificially generated rather than spontaneously produced.

A class-action suit is building against SynapTech after it emerges that ReadRoom Pro's SocialGraph model was trained partly on non-consenting biometric data harvested from public surveillance — and the players are hired to either expose the data pipeline or bury it.

A hostage negotiator's ReadRoom Pro is remotely fed false emotional data during a critical standoff, making a cooperative subject appear deceptive and a deceptive one appear calm. Someone wanted the negotiation to fail.
